habitat: Golden toads were endemic to a single, tiny area of cloud forest — the Monteverde Cloud Forest Reserve in Costa Rica — at elevations of 1,500-1,700 meters. They inhabited the cool, misty, moss-draped cloud forests characterized by persistent fog, high humidity, and moderate year-round temperatures. They were found in burrows and under moss and leaf litter, emerging only during the breeding season. The species was last seen in 1989 and is now classified as Extinct — one of the first documented vertebrate extinctions directly linked to climate change.
diet: Golden toads were presumed to be insectivorous, feeding on small invertebrates such as ants, beetles, flies, and other forest floor arthropods. As with most toads, they likely employed a sit-and-wait hunting strategy, remaining motionless and using their projectile, sticky tongue to capture passing prey. Due to their brief above-ground activity period (limited to the breeding season), their feeding biology was never thoroughly studied before their extinction.
behavior: Golden toads were subterranean and secretive, spending most of the year in underground burrows, emerging only during the April-June breeding season of heavy rains. Breeding aggregations were spectacular — hundreds of brilliant orange males would gather at temporary pools, competing intensely for females. Males outnumbered females by 10:1, leading to frenzied mating scrambles. Females laid 200-400 eggs in shallow water, which hatched into tadpoles that developed rapidly before the ephemeral pools dried up. The species disappeared so quickly that scientists never fully documented their life history.
facts: The golden toad is one of the most iconic symbols of amphibian extinction. The entire species vanished between 1987 and 1989 — a span of just two years. The cause is believed to be a combination of climate change (El Niño-driven drought affecting their cloud forest habitat), chytrid fungal disease, and habitat fragmentation. The last confirmed sighting was a single male in 1989. No golden toad has been seen since, despite extensive searches. Their brilliant orange coloration was sexually dimorphic — females were dark olive with scarlet spots, while males were a uniform, brilliant golden-orange. They are a cautionary tale of how rapidly a species can be lost.
naming: Golden toad names might honor their memory, reflect their brilliant color, or pay tribute to their Costa Rican home. Consider names like Aurelius (golden in Latin), Sol (sun), Costa, Monteverde, Amber, Oro (gold), Nube (cloud in Spanish), Ray, El Dorado, Solana (sunshine), Canario (canary), and Xanthus (yellow in Greek).
